chunks: I wrote to the man (peace be upon him) that those among us have disagreed concerning the Divine Unity (Tawhid) — among them is one who says 'He is a body,' and among them is one who says 'He is a form/image.'
So he wrote back to me: Glorified is the One Who cannot be limited, nor described, nor can anything resemble Him, and there is nothing like unto Him — and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

key_terms.التوحيد: Tawhid — the doctrine of Divine Unity; here specifically the question of God's nature and essence
key_terms.جسم: Body — the heretical view that God has a physical body, rejected by Shia theology
key_terms.سبحان: Glorified/Transcendent — an exclamation asserting God's absolute incomparability
key_terms.صورة: Image/form — another heretical view that God has a form or image resembling creation
key_terms.كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ: Anything like unto Him — direct quotation echoing Quran 42:11, the cornerstone of divine transcendence
key_terms.يُحَدُّ: To be limited/bounded — God transcends all limits and definitions
key_terms.يُوصَفُ: To be described — God cannot be adequately described by human language

ai.seo_question: What did the Imam say about God having a body or form in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Bishr ibn Bashshar al-Naysaburi wrote to the Imam (likely Imam al-Hadi, AS) about theological disputes in his community regarding the nature of God — some claiming God was a body (jism) and others saying He was an image (surah). The Imam's written reply rejects all anthropomorphism, echoing Quran 42:11, asserting divine transcendence: God cannot be limited, described, or compared to anything, for He alone is the All-Hearing and the All-Seeing. This hadith was transmitted in a cautious period when the Imam could not be publicly named, hence the use of the coded epithet 'al-Rajul' (the man).
